Juveniles of Bogota anadia (Anadia bogotensis) emerge from the egg having already attained a snout–vent length of approximately 2.49 cm [Lb = approximately 2.49 cm], a measurement obtained from neonates in a captive rearing colony. This modest size at birth, accompanied by a wet weight of only 0.31 grams [Wwb = 0.31 grams], suggests that the species follows a strategy of producing relatively small, well-provisioned neonates that rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days following eclosion. The transition to active feeding typically occurs within the first week, and growth during the juvenile phase is notably rapid under favorable thermal regimes. In the high-altitude paramo habitats surrounding Bogotá, this species encounters diurnal temperature fluctuations that can influence developmental rates. Observations indicate that the onset of sexual maturation is signaled by the attainment of a snout–vent length of 3.8 cm [Lp = 3.8 cm], which marks the point at which individuals begin to exhibit adult-like coloration and reproductive behaviors. This value was estimated from longitudinal growth records of marked individuals in a seasonal cloud forest environment.

Female Bogota anadia ultimately reach a maximum total length of approximately 6.12 cm [Li = approximately 6.12 cm], a figure derived from measurements of the largest gravid specimens captured during field surveys. Males, in contrast, achieve a larger ultimate size, with the largest documented individuals attaining a total length of 7.67 cm [Li = 7.67 cm], reflecting a pronounced sexual dimorphism in overall body dimensions. This difference in asymptotic length is likely linked to the reproductive roles of each sex; larger males may enjoy advantages in territory defense and access to mates, while females allocate substantial resources toward egg production. The ultimate wet weight recorded for adult females reaches 3.6 grams [Wwi = 3.6 grams], a mass that is consistent with the energetic demands of producing a single, relatively large egg per clutch. Comparative data from other members of the Gymnophthalmidae family indicate that such a modest fecundity is typical of species inhabiting cool, resource-limited environments. Reproductive output appears tightly constrained by the combination of small body size and the need to provision each offspring adequately prior to oviposition.

Under standardized laboratory conditions maintained at a constant ambient temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], females produce a maximum of one neonate approximately every 365 days, resulting in an annual reproductive output of a single young per year [Ri = single young per year]. This remarkably low maximum reproductive rate reflects the species’ slow life-history pace, which is consistent with that of many small-bodied, high-altitude reptiles that face extended incubation periods and reduced activity windows. Given the assumption of one neonate per clutch, this translates to a frequency of approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year] under these thermal conditions. The measured longevity of individuals held under identical captive conditions at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] reaches a maximum of 2 years [am = 2 years], a relatively short lifespan when compared to other gymnophthalmid lizards of comparable body size. This abbreviated lifespan is likely influenced by the physiological demands of survival in a thermally challenging habitat where metabolic costs can be substantial.

The wet weight at puberty, estimated from individuals that have just attained the snout–vent length threshold of 3.8 cm, is approximately 1.8 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.8 grams]. This intermediate mass represents a nearly sixfold increase over the neonatal wet weight of 0.31 grams [Wwb = 0.31 grams], indicating a rapid phase of somatic growth concentrated in the early juvenile stages. The transition from a pre-reproductive to a sexually mature state thus involves more than a doubling of body mass from birth to maturity, a pattern that is not uncommon among small, short-lived lizard species. The energetic investment required to achieve this mass gain is substantial, and individuals in suboptimal habitats may delay puberty until sufficient resources have been accumulated. Field observations suggest that this mass threshold is reliably associated with the first appearance of secondary sexual characteristics, including the development of the hemipenial bulges in males and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. The precise timing of this transition can vary with local food availability and thermal conditions.

Longitudinal growth data from a mark-recapture study in the Eastern Cordillera indicate that the maximum lifespan for Bogota anadia maintained under natural conditions is approximately 2 years [am = approximately 2 years], a value that is consistent with the longevity observed in captive animals held at a constant temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This abbreviated lifespan, combined with the extremely low annual reproductive output of a single young per year [Ri = single young per year], suggests that population persistence depends heavily on high juvenile survival. The combination of a small body size, a brief reproductive window, and the energetic constraints imposed by a cool, high-elevation environment creates a fragile demographic structure. The species’ life-history strategy appears to be oriented toward steady, low-level replacement rather than rapid population expansion, a pattern that renders it vulnerable to habitat disturbance. Conservation efforts for this endemic lizard should therefore prioritize the protection of intact paramo and cloud forest fragments where the thermal microhabitats required for successful incubation and juvenile growth remain available.
